ramuz-charles-ferdinand: Skomlin publishes six of Ramuz's novels in English, more than any other press in the language. The list runs from The Reign of the Evil One, the first of his books to reach English readers, in 1922, through Beauty on Earth, What if the sun..., Derborence and Farinet's Gold, and includes his only long prose poem, Riversong of the Rhone, in a bilingual edition.
bailat-jones-michelle: Michelle Bailat-Jones has translated two of the six Ramuz novels Skomlin publishes. Beauty on Earth, which Ramuz finished in 1927, had waited decades for an English translation. What if the sun... had never appeared in English at all, and her edition carries both the 1937 novel and the 1912 short story it grew from.
spinney-laura: Laura Spinney appears twice on the Skomlin list in two different roles: as the translator of Derborence, and as the author of the foreword to What if the sun...
garnett-constance: Constance Garnett translated the whole of Turgenev into English in the fifteen volumes of The Novels of Ivan Turgenev, published between 1894 and 1899. Skomlin publishes two of those stories in her texts, King Lear of the Steppes and The Diary of a Superfluous Man.
turgenev-ivan: Two of Turgenev's shorter works, both in Constance Garnett's translations. King Lear of the Steppes moves Shakespeare's tragedy onto a Russian estate. The Diary of a Superfluous Man gave Russian literature the phrase it still uses for a certain kind of wasted life.
leskov-nikolai: Two Leskov tales in their early English translations. Lady Macbeth of the Mtsensk District is the story Shostakovich made into an opera, written, Leskov said, in a punishment room at Kiev university. Cross-eyed Lefty and the Steel Flea is its opposite in every way, a folk satire on Russian pride told in the voice of a village storyteller.
hesse-hermann: Two of Hesse's shorter novels, both in Hilda Rosner's translations, and both circling the same question of how a person finds their own way to the truth rather than being taught it. Siddhartha follows a Brahmin's son from indulgence to asceticism and past both. The Journey to the East follows a pilgrimage that falls apart in a mountain gorge.
rosner-hilda: Hilda Rosner's translations carried Hermann Hesse into English and have stayed in print for more than seventy years. Skomlin publishes two of them, Siddhartha and The Journey to the East.
kraszewski-j-zef-ignacy: Two of Kraszewski's Saxon novels, both set around the court of Augustus the Strong in Dresden and Warsaw. Countess Cosel follows the king's mistress into a prison she never left. Count Bruhl follows the minister whose ambition helped bankrupt Poland. Kraszewski wrote more than two hundred novels; these are among the few available in English.
de-savoy-carignan-guy-jean-raoul-euge: Both Kraszewski novels on the Skomlin list are his translations, made at the turn of the twentieth century, when almost no Polish fiction was reaching English readers at all.
dos-passos-john: Two early Dos Passos books, written before the U.S.A. trilogy made his name. One Man's Initiation: 1917 was his first novel, drawn from the diaries he kept as an ambulance driver on the Western Front, and it sold 63 copies in its first six months. Rosinante to the Road Again follows two travellers on foot from Madrid to Toledo.
rychlowska-marianna: Two of the Polish titles on the Skomlin list carry introductions by Marianna Rychlowska, supplying the biographical and historical context that the first readers of Hoffmanowa and Reymont would have taken for granted. The introduction to The Comedienne also includes a history of the early Polish theatre.
